ACTION:

SUMMARY:

Pursuant to the Act, interested parties are requested to respond to this notice by submitting the information specified below to the Commission.

Background.
—On December 14, 2021, the Department of Commerce (“Commerce”) issued antidumping duty orders on imports of polyester textured yarn from Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam (86 FR 71031). Provisions concerning the conduct of this proceeding may be found in the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure at 19 CFR part 201, subparts A and B, and 19 CFR part 207, subparts A and F. Definitions.

is the class or kind of merchandise that is within the scope of the five-year reviews, as defined by Commerce.

Domestic Like Product

Subject Merchandise.

Domestic Industry

Domestic Like Product,

Domestic Like Product

Domestic Industry
as all producers of polyester textured yarn.
(5) The
Order Date
is the date that the antidumping duty orders under review became effective. In these reviews, the
Order Date
is December 14, 2021.
(6) An
Importer
is any person or firm engaged, either directly or through a parent company or subsidiary, in importing the
Subject Merchandise
into the United States from a foreign manufacturer or through its selling agent.

Subject Merchandise

SUMMARY:
The Commission hereby gives notice of the scheduling of expedited reviews pursuant to the Tariff Act of 1930 (“the Act”) to determine whether revocation of the countervailing duty orders on utility scale wind towers from India and Malaysia and the antidumping duty orders on utility scale wind towers from India, Malaysia, and Spain would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury within a reasonably foreseeable time.
DATES:
October 5, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Laurel Schwartz—(202) 205-2398), Office of Investigations, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436. Hearing-impaired persons can obtain information on this matter by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on 202-205-1810. Persons with mobility impairments who will need special assistance in gaining access to the Commission should contact the Office of the Secretary at 202-205-2000. General information concerning the Commission may also be obtained by accessing its internet server (
https://www.usitc.gov). The public record for this proceeding may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at
https://edis.usitc.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background.
—On October 5, 2026, the Commission determined that the domestic interested party group response to its notice of institution (91 FR 40578, July 2, 2026) of the subject five-year reviews was adequate and that the domestic interested party group response was inadequate. The Commission did not find any other circumstances that would warrant conducting full reviews.[1]
Accordingly, the Commission determined that it would conduct expedited reviews pursuant to section 751(c)(3) of the Act (19 U.S.C. 1675(c)(3)).[2]
For further information concerning the conduct of these reviews and rules of general application, consult the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure, part 201, subparts A and B (19 CFR part 201), and part 207, subparts A, D, E, and F (19 CFR part 207).
Staff report.
—A staff report containing information concerning the subject matter of the reviews has been placed in the nonpublic record, and will be made available to persons on the Administrative Protective Order service list for these reviews on January 7, 2027. A public version will be issued thereafter, pursuant to § 207.62(d)(4) of the Commission's rules.
Written submissions.
—As provided in § 207.62(d) of the Commission's rules, interested parties that are parties to the reviews and that have provided individually adequate responses to the notice of institution,[3]
and any party other than an interested party to the reviews may file written comments with the Secretary on what determination the Commission should reach in the reviews. Comments are due on or before January 14, 2027 and may not contain
( printed page 68971)
new factual information. Any person that is neither a party to the five-year reviews nor an interested party may submit a brief written statement (which shall not contain any new factual information) pertinent to the reviews by January 14, 2027. However, should the Department of Commerce (“Commerce”) extend the time limit for its completion of the final results of its reviews, the deadline for comments (which may not contain new factual information) on Commerce's final results is three business days after the issuance of Commerce's results. If comments contain business proprietary information (BPI), they must conform with the requirements of §§ 201.6, 207.3, and 207.7 of the Commission's rules. The Commission's
Handbook on Filing Procedures, available on the Commission's website at
https://www.usitc.gov/documents/handbook_on_filing_procedures.pdf, elaborates upon the Commission's procedures with respect to filings.
In accordance with §§ 201.16(c) and 207.3 of the rules, each document filed by a party to the reviews must be served on all other parties to the reviews (as identified by either the public or BPI service list), and a certificate of service must be timely filed. The Secretary will not accept a document for filing without a certificate of service.
Determination.
—The Commission has determined these reviews are extraordinarily complicated and therefore has determined to exercise its authority to extend the review period by up to 90 days pursuant to 19 U.S.C. 1675(c)(5)(B).
Authority:
These reviews are being conducted under authority of title VII of the Tariff Act of 1930; this notice is published pursuant to § 207.62 of the Commission's rules.
By order of the Commission.

high_priority_articles.summary: Philippines Snubs China at ASEAN Defense Meeting Amid South China Sea Tensions  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Lapu-Lapu City, Philippines — Defense leaders from across the Indo-Pacific gathered in Cebu this week for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) premier defense diplomacy events, but the proceedings were overshadowed by a deliberate diplomatic snub directed at Beijing and escalating maritime confrontations in the South China Sea.
The 20th ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) and the 13th ADMM-Plus, held on October 28 and 29, served as a critical platform for regional security dialogue. However, the host nation, the Philippines, utilized its 2026 ASEAN Chairmanship to firmly align the bloc’s security architecture with international maritime law, directly challenging China’s expansive territorial claims.
A Calculated Diplomatic Distance
The most visible manifestation of the strained relations occurred during the ADMM-Plus plenary sessions, which include eight key dialogue partners such as the United States, Japan, and Australia. Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro notably excluded Chinese representatives from key bilateral and minilateral security consultations on the sidelines of the summit.
Diplomatic sources in Cebu confirmed that Manila deliberately bypassed standard courtesy engagements with the Chinese delegation, a move interpreted as a direct response to recent aggressive maneuvers by Chinese coast guard vessels against Philippine resupply missions in the disputed Second Thomas Shoal and Sabina Shoal. The snub signals a hardening of Manila’s posture, shifting away from the traditional ASEAN consensus of quiet diplomacy toward a more confrontational, rules-based approach to regional security.
South China Sea Dominates the Agenda
While the official communiqué emphasized ASEAN unity and non-traditional security threats like disaster response and cyber defense, the closed-door sessions were dominated by the deteriorating situation in the West Philippine Sea. Defense ministers from Vietnam, Malaysia, and Indonesia reportedly expressed strong support for the Philippines’ insistence on upholding the 2016 arbitral ruling, which invalidated China’s nine-dash line claim.
The presence of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and other Plus partners underscored the internationalization of the dispute. The United States reiterated its ironclad commitments under the Mutual Defense Treaty, warning that any armed attack on Philippine public vessels in the South China Sea would trigger a US response. This explicit security guarantee has emboldened Manila to take a harder line within ASEAN forums, frustrating Chinese diplomats who have long sought to keep the dispute strictly bilateral and isolated from multilateral security architectures.
Regional Threats and Strategic Realignment
Beyond the maritime disputes, the Cebu meetings addressed a broader spectrum of regional threats, including the proliferation of advanced military technologies and the deepening strategic partnership between Beijing and Moscow. ASEAN members expressed concern over the potential deployment of dual-use technologies and the militarization of artificial islands, which they argue destabilizes the regional balance of power.
The ADMM-Plus also focused on enhancing interoperability among partner nations for humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR), a relatively neutral area where cooperation with China is still maintained. However, the underlying strategic divergence was palpable. While China advocated for an "Asian security model" led by regional powers without external interference, the Philippines and its Western partners pushed for an "open, inclusive, and rules-based" architecture that explicitly welcomes the continued presence of external powers to balance regional hegemony.
As the summit concluded, the message from Cebu was unequivocal. The Philippines, leveraging its chairmanship, has successfully shifted the center of gravity within ASEAN’s defense establishment. By openly snubbing Beijing and deepening military integration with the US and its allies, Manila is betting that collective deterrence and international legal frameworks offer a more viable path to securing its sovereign rights than the traditional ASEAN doctrine of non-interference and consensus-driven accommodation.
The implications of the Cebu meetings extend far beyond the immediate diplomatic theater. For smaller ASEAN states, the Philippine strategy presents both an opportunity and a risk. While it provides a stronger collective voice against coercion, it also raises the specter of forcing member states to choose sides in an intensifying great-power rivalry. Indonesia and Singapore, traditionally the architects of ASEAN’s hedging strategy, spent much of the summit attempting to bridge the gap between Manila’s assertiveness and the desire of other members to maintain stable economic ties with Beijing.
Ultimately, the 2026 ADMM cycle will be remembered as the moment the Philippines successfully weaponized its ASEAN chairmanship to redraw the region's security fault lines, ensuring that the South China Sea remains the defining geopolitical flashpoint of the Indo-Pacific.

high_priority_articles.title: Latest IMF Forecast: Vietnam's GDP Per Capita to Surpass Indonesia's for First Time in 2026, Rising to Fifth in ASEAN - BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.summary: Latest IMF Forecast: Vietnam's GDP Per Capita to Surpass Indonesia's for First Time in 2026, Rising to Fifth in ASEAN  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The International Monetary Fund's (IMF) latest forecast shows that Vietnam's nominal GDP per capita will reach $5,259 in 2026, up 8.9% from the previous year, surpassing Indonesia's $5,153 for the first time. This turning point means Vietnam will rise to fifth place among ASEAN member states in GDP per capita, trailing only Thailand.
Vietnam's population is currently about 100 million, while Indonesia's is about 290 million—nearly a threefold difference—making this crossover in the per-capita indicator particularly noteworthy. GDP per capita is calculated by dividing total GDP by population; nominal values are measured at current prices without inflation adjustment and are also affected by exchange-rate fluctuations when converted into dollars.
Vietnam's growth momentum stems mainly from its gradual emergence as a high-tech manufacturing base alternative to China. As supply chains for electronic components and semiconductors accelerate their relocation, international industry giants such as Taiwan's Hon Hai Group (2317.TW) and South Korea's Samsung Electronics are continuing to expand production in Vietnam, driving large-scale exports of smartphones and other electronic products.
Export and foreign investment data reflect this trend. In the first nine months of this year, Vietnam's exports reached $434.3 billion, up 25% year-on-year; foreign direct investment (FDI) reached $21.1 billion, up 12% year-on-year. Registered capital, a leading indicator of investment, surged 76% to $50.3 billion, showing that foreign investors' long-term commitment to Vietnam has not cooled.
Public infrastructure is another core engine. Vietnam plans to invest about VND 1,000 trillion (approximately $38.8 billion) in 2026 to advance nationwide roads, airports and other infrastructure. Mai Fujita, a senior researcher at Japan's Institute of Developing Economies, noted: "The Vietnamese government's active public investment is supporting economic growth."
On growth, Vietnam's government has set a target of at least 10% economic growth in 2026, while the IMF's latest report forecasts 8.4% growth for Vietnam in 2026, the highest in Southeast Asia. By comparison, Indonesia's growth remains around 5%, with a forecast of 5.1% for 2026.
Although Indonesia has worked hard to attract foreign investment in industries such as electric vehicles, those funds have not effectively translated into sufficient jobs and real income growth, and a weaker rupiah has curbed the growth of its dollar-denominated nominal GDP per capita.
Looking ahead, Vietnam has set a target of raising GDP per capita to $8,500 by 2030, equivalent to Thailand's current level. Fujita believes that beyond short-term infrastructure investment to stimulate growth, Vietnam also needs to "strive for long-term growth, such as developing human resources and technology."
For investors, the forecast highlights that ASEAN's manufacturing landscape is being reshaped. Vietnam is catching up rapidly with an export-oriented, foreign-investment-driven model, while Indonesia faces the challenge of turning foreign investment into real wage growth. The golden crossover in the two countries' per-capita income will also become an important indicator for regional supply-chain positioning and capital flows.
Note: GDP per capita figures are nominal values, calculated at current prices without inflation adjustment, and are affected by exchange-rate movements when converted into dollars.

Sudan’s Sovereignty Council Chairman, General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, has offered Russia access to investment opportunities in the country’s strategic Red Sea corridor, gold and copper mining sectors, as Khartoum seeks to deepen economic cooperation with Moscow.
Al-Burhan made the proposals during bilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, outlining opportunities for Russian investment in mineral extraction, fuel storage, grain logistics and regional trade infrastructure.
“Sudan can provide Russia with a gateway to the Red Sea,” al-Burhan said, highlighting his country’s strategic location along one of the world’s major maritime trade routes.
He said Sudan was prepared to strengthen relations with Moscow amid changing international and domestic circumstances.
“Given global and domestic developments, we need more than ever to develop mutually beneficial cooperation between our countries,” he said.
“Today’s Sudanese government has the political will and will work hard on cooperation with Russia.”
The Sudanese leader proposed establishing Russian grain and petroleum storage facilities in Sudan, positioning the country as a potential distribution hub for commodities destined for other African markets.
“Russia could set up grain and fuel storage facilities in Sudan; we have the capacity and the means to do so,” he said.
“There is demand for these commodities across the entire African continent, and we have the potential to develop supply chains towards the Chad region.”
The discussions come as Sudan seeks foreign investment to rebuild an economy devastated by more than three years of civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
The conflict, which erupted in April 2023, has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced millions and severely damaged Sudan’s infrastructure
Al-Burhan said Sudan possessed the land and infrastructure potential to support such projects but required foreign capital to bring them into operation.
“We have the land and the means; what we need is investment, and we are very eager to work with Russia in this area,” he said.
The proposals also extend to Sudan’s mining industry, particularly gold and copper, with Khartoum indicating that specific mineral deposits have already been identified for potential Russian investment.
“We currently have areas we are ready to hand over to Russia for investment,” al-Burhan said.
“I am talking about copper and gold mining, and I sincerely assure you that we are ready to cooperate in this area.”
He also emphasised Sudan’s sovereignty over its economic decisions, rejecting suggestions that foreign governments could dictate the country’s investment priorities.
“No country dictates any agenda to us; everything comes from Sudan, and we are in full control,” he said.
Putin speaks out
Putin, meanwhile, described Sudan as an “important Russian partner in Africa and the Arab world”, saying bilateral trade more than doubled in 2025 and grew by another 25% between January and August 2026.
He said Moscow had prepared a roadmap for cooperation covering digital technology, healthcare, education, logistics and industry.
The Russian leader also called for an end to hostilities in Sudan and a political settlement to the conflict. ￼
Sudan’s offer of a Red Sea economic zone is particularly significant given Russia’s longstanding interest in establishing a presence along the strategic waterway, which connects international shipping routes between Europe, Asia and Africa.
However, the investment proposals remain subject to further negotiations, and no final agreements on the proposed facilities or mining concessions were announced following the talks. ￼
The meeting formed part of Moscow’s broader diplomatic engagement with African countries during the October 28–29 summit, which brought together representatives from 48 African nations to discuss trade, investment, infrastructure and security cooperation.

high_priority_articles.title: US, South Korea and Japan Reaffirm Commitment to North Korea’s ‘Complete Denuclearization’ - Opinion Nigeria
high_priority_articles.summary: US, South Korea and Japan Reaffirm Commitment to North Korea’s ‘Complete Denuclearization’  Opinion Nigeria
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The United States, South Korea and Japan have renewed their commitment to the “complete denuclearization” of North Korea as Pyongyang continues to reject disarmament ahead of possible nuclear talks with Washington.
Speculation has grown over a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China, following repeated overtures by Trump for renewed nuclear negotiations.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reaffirmed their position during a meeting on Friday on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) gathering in Atlanta, Georgia.
According to the US State Department, the three officials “reaffirmed their resolute commitment to the complete denuclearization” of North Korea.
They also pledged to ensure the “full implementation” of United Nations Security Council resolutions, including measures prohibiting support for revenue-generating activities linked to North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programmes.
Despite years of international sanctions, North Korea, which enjoys support from Russia and China, has legally entrenched its status as a nuclear-armed state. Its government has repeatedly insisted that its nuclear arsenal is permanent and irreversible.
Trump open to meeting Kim
Trump has repeatedly expressed willingness to engage Pyongyang in nuclear negotiations while reducing joint military exercises with South Korea, a key US ally.
The US president departed from longstanding American policy last year when he acknowledged that North Korea was already “sort of a nuclear power”. He also signalled that he was “100 percent” open to meeting Kim, although the North Korean leader did not respond to the proposal.
Analysts and South Korea’s intelligence agency believe Kim may have communicated Pyongyang’s position on possible talks with Trump to Beijing during a recent visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong.
South Korea’s President Lee Jae Myung, who has adopted a more conciliatory approach towards Pyongyang, has repeatedly called for dialogue without preconditions.
In September, Lee suggested that Washington consider pursuing a freeze on North Korea’s nuclear programme rather than demanding its immediate dismantlement, in exchange for sanctions relief.
However, critics argue that such a proposal could amount to tacit recognition of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state while allowing Pyongyang to secure sanctions relief without surrendering its weapons.
Some analysts also believe China may be moving towards accepting North Korea’s nuclear status, citing the absence of references to denuclearisation in statements issued after Kim met Chinese President Xi Jinping in June.
Meanwhile, Pyongyang on Saturday criticised a joint statement issued by a group of countries monitoring the implementation of sanctions against it.
North Korea insisted that “the stereotyped sanctions racket of the US and the West can neither influence the position of the DPRK (North Korea) as a nuclear weapons state”.

According to a joint statement from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the U.S. Department of State, and Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi held a trilateral meeting for approximately 20 minutes starting at 5:05 p.m. in Atlanta, where the G20 (20 countries) foreign ministers’ meeting was taking place.

The MSMT was newly established by 11 countries, including South Korea, the U.S., and Japan, after the UN expert panel, which had been investigating North Korea’s sanctions violations, was dissolved in 2024 due to Russia’s veto in the Security Council.
The three ministers also agreed to maintain a robust deterrence posture against North Korea through close coordination and to continue solidarity in addressing malicious cyber activities that fund North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs. The U.S. Department of State noted that Secretary Rubio highlighted a “free and open Indo-Pacific,” raising concerns about China’s attempts to strengthen control over the South China Sea, coercive behavior in the East China Sea and Yellow Sea, and Russia-China cooperation undermining peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region. high_priority_articles.title: President Directs Section 232 Negotiations on Robotics and Industrial Machinery Imports, Defers Tariffs or Quotas - Thompson Hine
high_priority_articles.summary: President Directs Section 232 Negotiations on Robotics and Industrial Machinery Imports, Defers Tariffs or Quotas  Thompson Hine
high_priority_articles.full_text:
On October 28, 2026, President Trump issued a proclamation titled “Adjusting Imports of Robotics, Industrial Machinery, and Their Parts and Components into the United States,” directing the Secretary of Commerce and the United States Trade Representative (USTR) to jointly pursue negotiations with trading partners to address the national security threat posed by these imports. Rather than imposing tariffs or quotas now, the proclamation makes negotiated agreements the initial remedy.
The action follows a Commerce investigation initiated under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1862) (see Update of September 25, 2025). The Secretary found that robotics, industrial machinery, and their parts and components “are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States,” and the President concurred.
According to the proclamation, the Secretary found that:
- robotics and industrial machinery support production of defense systems such as aircraft, tanks, ships, weapons, and munitions;
- robotics and industrial machines are crucial to the United States’ critical infrastructure sectors and other key aspects of the United States economy;
- the United States relies on foreign imports for most types of robotics and industrial machinery and their components, and the value of those imports has increased over the last decade;
- robotics and machinery from “certain foreign entities pose unique security and safety risks,” including cybersecurity vulnerabilities, because they routinely process and store sensitive data; and
- domestic industry does not produce enough of these products to meet national security needs.
The proclamation states that, “[d]epending on the status or outcome of such negotiations,” the President “may consider alternative remedies in the future, including imposing or modifying tariffs, duties, quotas, and fees; and establishing a program to incentivize new investment in United States production of robotics and industrial machinery, as well as their parts and components.” It also notes that, under 19 U.S.C. 1862(c)(3)(A), the President may take other actions “to adjust imports to eliminate the threat that the imported article poses to the national security” if an agreement is not entered into within 180 days, is not being carried out, or is ineffective.
The Secretary and USTR must update the President on the negotiations within 180 days of the date of the proclamation. Importers and manufacturers that rely on imported robotics and industrial machinery should consider monitoring these negotiations, as tariffs, quotas, fees, or other actions remain possible.
Notably, the security concerns regarding foreign-sourced robotics echo recent Federal Communications Commission (FCC) actions adding advanced robotic devices and power inverters to the FCC Covered List (see Update of August 4, 2026; see also Update of August 26, 2026).

On October 30th, in Hanoi, the Ministry of Industry and Trade held a meeting with major electronics businesses to assess the production and import-export situation, clarify the causes of the trade deficit, and discuss the industry's development prospects in the coming period.
Electronics exports surged, but the trade deficit remained large.
In his opening remarks, Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade Luong Hoang Thai acknowledged and highly appreciated the efforts of the electronics business community, while emphasizing the role of this industry in Vietnam's export activities.
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
According to information from the Import-Export Department of the Ministry of Industry and Trade, it is estimated that Vietnam's total import and export turnover in the first 10 months of 2026 reached US$1,010.6 billion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period in 2025, officially surpassing the US$1 trillion mark. In October alone, import and export turnover is estimated at US$122.2 billion, an increase of 47.6% compared to the same period last year.
Notably, exports continued to grow strongly, with estimated turnover reaching $499 billion in the first 10 months, an increase of 27.4%, creating positive momentum to achieve and surpass the export growth target of 15-16% for the whole year of 2026.
Khám phá thêm
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch
Khám phá ĐNA
In the import-export structure, the electronics industry continues to affirm its position as one of the leading industries, making a significant contribution to the country's export turnover.
According to data from the Customs Department, Ministry of Finance , as of October 15, 2026, the cumulative export value of the two product groups, computers, electronic products and components; and telephones of all types and components, reached US$189.65 billion, accounting for approximately 40% of the country's total export value.
Specifically, the group of computers, electronic products, and components reached $135.3 billion, a 65% increase compared to the same period in 2025. According to assessments presented at the meeting, the increasing demand for artificial intelligence ( AI ) equipment and data centers globally is one of the factors driving the export growth of this product group.

However, despite positive export results, the trade balance of the electronics industry is raising concerns. Specifically, the total import value of the two major electronics product groups reached $209.7 billion. Of this, imports of computers, electronic products, and components reached approximately $201 billion, resulting in a trade deficit of $65.69 billion for this group.
Although the group of telephones and components recorded a trade surplus of over $45.67 billion, the overall trade balance of the two product groups still showed a deficit of approximately $20 billion.
Notably, after 10 consecutive years of maintaining a trade surplus, Vietnam's trade balance shifted to a deficit in 2026. This development necessitates a more thorough assessment of the import-export structure, especially for the electronics industry – a sector with high export value but currently recording a significant deficit.
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Finding solutions to the electronics industry's trade deficit problem.
At the meeting, Mr. Tran Thanh Hai, Deputy Director of the Import-Export Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade), presented an overview of the production, import-export situation and development prospects of Vietnam's electronics industry.
“ Vietnam has become one of the important electronics manufacturing locations in the global supply chain, with the presence of many large corporations such as Samsung , LG, Intel, Foxconn, and Canon,” Mr. Tran Thanh Hai emphasized.
However, the production structure of the electronics industry remains clearly differentiated. While foreign-invested enterprises (FDI) play a dominant role in manufacturing, assembly, and export, domestic enterprises mainly participate in component production, supporting industries, and providing technical services.
Notably, one of the reasons for the trade deficit is the sharp increase in demand for imported raw materials and components for production. Some types of chips have seen price increases of 300-500%, causing a significant increase in import value even when import volume has not increased proportionally.
In addition, businesses are increasing their accumulation and stockpiling of raw materials and components to support production plans, while simultaneously expanding factory scale, production lines, and exports. This leads to a demand for importing machinery, equipment, and input materials.
Another issue highlighted is that electronics manufacturing in Vietnam remains heavily reliant on imported components and raw materials, while the localization rate and added value generated domestically are limited.

This also includes the need to diversify markets and supply sources, improve the quality of human resources and logistics capabilities, aiming to transform Vietnam from a manufacturing and assembly center into a higher-value link in the global electronics supply chain.
Speaking at the meeting, Deputy Minister Luong Hoang Thai requested that businesses and delegates focus on analyzing the current state of development in the electronics industry, clarifying the causes of the trade deficit, and assessing the prospects for production, import, and export in the coming period. high_priority_articles.summary: Gulf shipping crisis deepens as Iran reports tanker fires, Houthis hit Saudi oil facilities  The News Pakistan
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said four oil tankers had caught fire and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz, while separate maritime security reports pointed to further attacks on commercial shipping, as the widening conflict involving Iran, the United States and Israel continued to threaten critical energy infrastructure across the Gulf.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the tankers had attempted to navigate routes it described as unauthorised. In its latest statement, it reported that a fourth vessel, carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil, had struck a naval mine, suffered a powerful explosion and caught fire, Iranian state media reported on Friday.
An earlier IRGC Navy statement had reported that another tanker carrying two million barrels of crude had struck a mine.
Reuters could not independently verify the Iranian military's account.
Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said it had received a report that a crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while completing an outbound transit through the strait.
In an earlier incident report, UKMTO said a vessel had been hit on its port side about 40 nautical miles (74km) south of Iran's Lavan Island, triggering a fire on board. Its crew were reported safe, with no environmental impact.
It was not immediately clear whether the vessels involved in the UKMTO reports were among the four tankers cited by Iran.
In a separate report on Friday, Reuters said UKMTO had reported a tanker being struck by explosive devices attached to a small boat, in what maritime sources described as the first known successful limpet-mine attack in the waterway since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February.
The incidents underline the growing dangers to commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage connecting the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea through which around a fifth of the world's oil supplies passed before the conflict.
Iranian state media also reported that its forces had downed and captured an MQM-170 US drone over Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate US military response to that claim, which Reuters could not independently verify.
Tehran also said it had destroyed an unmanned US vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.
However, the US military's Central Command rejected the claim, saying all American unmanned surface vessels in the Middle East were accounted for, including a squadron of advanced sea drones patrolling the waterway.
The latest maritime incidents come amid heightened tensions following US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February and subsequent Iranian attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure across the region.
Reuters reported earlier this month that Iran had shifted towards intensifying attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, seeking to keep oil prices elevated and increase pressure on Washington.
At least seven incidents involving tankers were reported during a week in early October, according to maritime intelligence service Marisks. The incidents included attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, raising concerns over the security of energy exports from the Gulf.
The maritime security crisis has coincided with a renewed Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia, further widening the conflict's geographical reach.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked several Saudi energy facilities, including the Ras Tanura refinery, the Rabigh refinery and a production facility at Abqaiq owned by state oil giant Saudi Aramco.
A Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom's western region.
The attacks followed repeated Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, oil installations and other critical infrastructure this month, including an October 10 attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, according to Reuters.
The Houthis have also threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, warning civilians, workers and international shipping companies to stay away from sites they consider legitimate targets.
The renewed offensive has severely disrupted Saudi aviation. According to aviation analytics firm Cirium, 4,071 of 4,736 scheduled flights at Riyadh's airport, or 86%, were cancelled between October 8 and October 25.
More than 7,800 flights, accounting for 45% of scheduled departures across Saudi airports, were cancelled during the same period.
The United States on Friday confirmed that it had ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia, effective October 23, citing security risks from Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure.
The US embassy in Riyadh warned American citizens of possible further attacks, airspace closures, flight cancellations and other travel disruptions.
The fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has intensified in recent weeks, opening another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.
A truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition collapsed in July. The group subsequently declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, attacked Saudi vessels and the East-West pipeline, and seized Yemen's Red Sea coastline and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to Reuters.
The military escalation has continued despite diplomatic efforts involving regional powers to prevent the conflict from spreading further.
Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday as part of coordinated efforts to reach an agreement between Washington and Tehran, an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Iran to help the country obtain medical supplies, following reports that Vance had written to Tehran's top security official in an effort to revive peace negotiations.
Iran has confirmed receiving Vance's letter but has yet to respond, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. Tehran has said Washington must meet its conditions for an agreement.
Earlier this week, Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials met Iranian leaders in Tehran and agreed to continue discussions, although the agenda and substance of the talks have not been disclosed.
Pakistan's military said on Friday it was "cautiously optimistic" about Islamabad's mediation efforts, following two visits to Tehran this month by Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin accompanied Munir during his latest visit.
The diplomatic engagement comes against the backdrop of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7, under which an attack on any signatory is to be treated as an attack on all.
Pakistan's military spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said the agreement did not rule out additional members, including Iran, although any expansion would require a decision by the signatories' political leadership.
The mounting security risks have added to concerns over global energy supplies, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining a critical chokepoint for crude oil and fuel shipments.
Oil prices rose more than 2% on Friday, settling at their highest levels since late April as traders weighed the possibility of further escalation and the risks to supplies from the Middle East.
Brent crude futures for December delivery settled $2.76 higher, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate rose $2.12, or 2.08%, to $104.12.
For October, Brent gained 13.6%, while WTI rose 15.2%.
The attacks have raised concerns about the ability of Gulf producers to maintain exports through both the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, particularly as Saudi Arabia faces renewed threats to its oil infrastructure and Red Sea shipping access.
Saudi crude exports nevertheless increased in October compared with September, according to two of three ship-tracking companies cited by Reuters, despite Iranian attacks on shipping and Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi energy facilities.
With Washington and Tehran yet to reach an agreement, the combination of maritime attacks, renewed fighting in Yemen and threats to Gulf energy infrastructure continues to complicate diplomatic efforts to contain the eight-month-old conflict.

Each year during the anniversary month of the publication of an antidumping duty (AD) or countervailing duty (CVD) order, finding, or suspended investigation, an interested party, as defined in section 771(9) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as

In the event Commerce decides it is necessary to limit individual examination of respondents and conduct respondent selection under section 777A(c)(2) of the Act:
1. In general, Commerce finds that determinations concerning whether particular companies should be “collapsed” (
i.e.,

Accordingly, Commerce will not conduct collapsing analyses at the respondent selection phase of a review and will not collapse companies at the respondent selection phase unless there has been a determination to collapse certain companies in a previous segment of this AD proceeding (

investigation, administrative review, new shipper review, or changed circumstances review).
2. For any company subject to a review, if Commerce determined, or continued to treat, that company as collapsed with others, Commerce will assume that such companies continue to operate in the same manner and will collapse them for respondent selection purposes. Otherwise, Commerce will not collapse companies for purposes of respondent selection.
3. Parties are requested to: (a) identify which companies subject to review previously were collapsed; and (b) provide a citation to the proceeding in which they were collapsed.
4. Deadline for Withdrawal of Request for Administrative Review
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(1), a party that requests a review may withdraw that request within 90 days of the date of publication of the notice of initiation of the requested review. The regulation provides that Commerce may extend this time if it is reasonable to do so. Determinations by Commerce to extend the 90-day deadline will be made on a case-by-case basis.
Deadline for Particular Market Situation Allegation
Section 504 of the Trade Preferences Extension Act of 2015 amended the Act by adding the concept of particular market situation (PMS) for purposes of constructed value under section 773(e) of the Act.[1]

If Commerce finds that a PMS exists under section 773(e) of the Act, then it will modify its dumping calculations appropriately.
Neither section 773(e) of the Act nor 19 CFR 351.301(c)(2)(v) set a deadline for the submission of PMS allegations and supporting factual information. Thus, should an interested party wish to submit a PMS allegation and supporting new factual information pursuant to section 773(e) of the Act, it must do so no later than 20 days after submission of initial Section D responses.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Key Highlights
- Recent central-bank assessments report that advanced-economy sovereign bond yields have risen since mid-year and that global financial conditions have tightened amid persistent Inflation and uncertainty.
- Higher benchmark yields raise financing costs for governments, companies and households. They can reduce the present value of future corporate cash flows, pressure property valuations and increase Mortgage rates. For savers, higher yields may improve income opportunities, but mark-to-market losses can affect existing bond portfolios and institutions with duration exposure.
- Watch inflation breakevens, auction demand, term premiums, fiscal announcements, central-bank guidance and the shape of yield curves. A rise driven by stronger real growth has different implications from one driven by inflation uncertainty or concerns about Debt sustainability. Investors should assess duration, refinancing schedules and Liquidity rather than relying on headline yield levels alone.
What is driving the latest development?
Government bond markets are adjusting to a world in which inflation may remain above target for longer and central banks cannot promise rapid easing. Investors are also assessing the Supply of government debt, fiscal credibility and the compensation required to hold long-duration securities. These forces can push yields higher even when economic growth is not accelerating.
The latest figures provide a useful starting point, but they should be interpreted in context. Economic data can be revised, seasonal patterns can distort short-term comparisons and national averages can conceal differences between sectors and households. Information available as of 30 October 2026 is the current evidence base, not a guarantee of the next outcome.
Higher benchmark yields raise financing costs for governments, companies and households. They can reduce the present value of future corporate cash flows, pressure property valuations and increase mortgage rates. For savers, higher yields may improve income opportunities, but mark-to-market losses can affect existing bond portfolios and institutions with duration exposure.
Watch inflation breakevens, auction demand, term premiums, fiscal announcements, central-bank guidance and the shape of yield curves. A rise driven by stronger real growth has different implications from one driven by inflation uncertainty or concerns about debt sustainability. Investors should assess duration, refinancing schedules and liquidity rather than relying on headline yield levels alone.
Why this matters now
The timing matters because markets and policymakers are making decisions with incomplete information. A single release can alter expectations, but the more durable signal comes from whether the same pattern appears in prices, activity, employment and financial conditions. Businesses should therefore avoid treating one headline number as a complete description of the cycle. The key current evidence is: Recent central-bank assessments report that advanced-economy sovereign bond yields have risen since mid-year and that global financial conditions have tightened amid persistent inflation and uncertainty.
How the transmission works
The economic transmission usually moves through several channels. First, the immediate change affects costs, income or confidence. Second, companies adjust orders, hiring, inventories and prices. Third, households respond through spending and saving, while lenders reassess risk and financing terms. The final effect on GDP can therefore lag the initial shock by several months. In this case, higher benchmark yields raise financing costs for governments, companies and households.
What it means for households
For households, the practical effect is felt through purchasing power, Job security, borrowing costs and the price of essentials. Even when headline growth is positive, a rise in unavoidable expenses can leave less room for discretionary purchases. The distribution of the impact matters: indebted households and people with limited savings are generally less able to absorb a prolonged period of higher costs. Government bond markets are adjusting to a world in which inflation may remain above target for longer and central banks cannot promise rapid easing.
What it means for businesses
For companies, planning assumptions should be revisited across input costs, demand, Working Capital and financing. Businesses with diversified suppliers, pricing flexibility and strong balance sheets may adapt more easily. Those dependent on imported inputs, short-term borrowing or a narrow customer base may face a more difficult adjustment. Scenario planning is more useful than relying on a single forecast.

high_priority_articles.title: Sweden’s Critical Minerals: Why Its Rare Earths Have No Mine Yet - Discovery Alert
high_priority_articles.summary: Sweden’s Critical Minerals: Why Its Rare Earths Have No Mine Yet  Discovery Alert
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
- LKAB lifted the Per Geijer resource to about 1.3 billion tonnes of iron and phosphorus, containing about 2.2 million tonnes of rare earth oxides, up from about 1.7 million tonnes.
- The Per Geijer rare earth component is only an Inferred Mineral Resource under PERC 2021, the lowest-confidence category, so it cannot be treated as a reserve or a producing mine.
- Swedish mines produced just under 80 million tonnes of ore in 2025, and Sweden supplies about 8% of EU copper, 42% of EU lead and 36% of EU zinc, but no rare earths.
- LKAB's ReeMAP, covering Malmberget and Per Geijer with processing at Luleå, won EU Strategic Project status in March 2025, which speeds permitting but does not guarantee a mine.
- Lithium, cobalt and nickel in Sweden remain occurrences and exploration targets, with no producing lithium mine or current lithium reserve found.
Sweden has one of Europe’s largest reported rare earth deposits, at roughly 2.2 million tonnes of rare earth oxides. Yet no Swedish mine is producing rare earths today. That gap between a headline tonnage and an actual operating mine is the most useful thing to understand about Sweden’s critical minerals story.
Most Swedish mining takes place in the Baltic Shield, also called the Fennoscandian Shield. It is the oldest rock in Europe and has supplied iron and base metals for more than a century.
The European Union’s critical raw materials policy has now turned attention to what else that bedrock might hold. Rare earths, lithium, cobalt and nickel all appear in Swedish geological surveys, and each one sits at a different stage of proof.
This explainer gives you a way to read any Swedish critical mineral headline. It covers where the rock comes from, what is actually mined, and what each classification label really tells you.
Why does the Baltic Shield host so much metal?
Start with the age. The Fennoscandian Shield is Precambrian crystalline bedrock, meaning old, hard rock formed before complex life appeared. Sweden’s main ore regions sit in the Svecokarelian orogen, a mountain-building belt formed roughly 2.0-1.8 billion years ago.
That belt was built through a long sequence of events: volcanic arcs, magma intrusions, folding, heating under pressure and later hot-fluid activity. The volcanic and intrusive rocks supplied the metals. The faults and altered zones gave mineral-rich fluids a path to travel and concentrate.
The Geological Survey of Sweden (SGU) names three principal ore districts in its 2026 National Exploration Programme: Northern Norrbotten, the Skellefte district and Bergslagen. Each district carries a different metal signature because a different part of that ancient sequence dominated there.
According to SGU, five features make the shield favourable:
- Volcanic arcs and submarine basins suited to sulphide deposits
- Intrusive and volcanic systems suited to iron-oxide-apatite deposits
- Long-lived deformation zones that moved and concentrated metals
- Widely exposed bedrock, which makes mapping and exploration easier
- Established infrastructure and processing expertise built around iron and sulphide mining
Iron-oxide-apatite deposits of Norrbotten
Kiruna, Malmberget, Svappavaara and Per Geijer are Kiruna-type iron-oxide-apatite deposits. They are dominated by magnetite or hematite, both iron oxides, alongside apatite, a mineral that contains phosphorus.
Apatite is the link to the critical minerals conversation. It can host rare earth elements, so iron mines in this setting carry potential by-product value beyond iron itself.
Your reading of Swedish headlines gets sharper once you separate rare metals and rare earths, because the two groups differ in extraction methods, supply chains and market behaviour, and a label like ‘critical’ can cover very different materials.
Volcanogenic massive sulphides of the Skellefte district
The Skellefte district is dominated by volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) deposits. These form when hot fluids from submarine volcanoes deposit metals on or below the seafloor, and here they mainly carry zinc, copper and lead with gold and silver.
Academic work places many of these deposits around the transition between the volcanic Skellefte Group and the overlying Vargfors Group. That boundary is the favourable setting explorers look for.
Key point: Geology creates prospectivity, not automatic economic supply.
You should read the shield’s age and structure as a reason to investigate Sweden’s critical mineral potential. Prospectivity says nothing yet about tonnage, grade or economics.

What does Sweden actually mine today?
Before weighing potential, it helps to see what the districts already deliver. According to SGU figures published in June 2026, Swedish mines produced just under 80 million tonnes of ore in 2025, roughly unchanged from 2024.
Iron ore output rose slightly. Base metal and gold production fell, while silver rose.
That output gives Sweden real weight in Europe. SGU reports Sweden’s share of EU production as:
- Approximately 8% of EU copper
- Approximately 42% of EU lead
- Approximately 36% of EU zinc

| Malmberget (LKAB) | Iron ore | Iron-oxide-apatite | Cumulative production about 640 million tonnes (SGU, 2026) | 
| Aitik (Boliden) | Copper, gold, silver | Porphyry copper | About 41 million tonnes of ore in 2023; about 1.03 billion tonnes cumulative, 1968-2023 | 
| Kristineberg, Renström, Kankberg (Boliden area) | Zinc, copper, lead, gold, silver | VMS, Skellefte district | No mine-specific 2025 figures found | 
| Garpenberg (Boliden) | Polymetallic sulphides | Bergslagen | No mine-specific 2025 figure found | 
Aitik shows why districts like these endure. A mine that started in 1968 passed a billion tonnes of cumulative production by 2023, helped by shared infrastructure, processing knowledge and continued resource work. The Boliden processing plant also treats ore from several Skellefte mines, which lets smaller, complex deposits keep operating.
You can use this as your benchmark. When a critical mineral project is described, compare its status with the decades of operating history behind these districts.
What is the difference between an occurrence, a resource and a mine?
Every mineral figure belongs to a rung on a classification ladder. Reporting codes such as JORC (Australia’s Joint Ore Reserves Committee Code) and the PERC Reporting Standard 2021, the European code referenced for current Swedish reporting, define what each rung means.
| Term | Meaning | What it does not prove | 
|---|---|---|
| Mineral occurrence | Documented presence of a mineral or raised element level | Tonnage, continuity, economic grade or mineability | 
| Historic estimate | Older estimate, often under a former code | May not qualify as a current compliant resource | 
| Inferred Resource | Lowest-confidence resource category | Cannot normally be treated as a reserve | 
| Indicated Resource | Enough confidence to evaluate mine planning | Still needs economic, legal, environmental and technical success | 
| Measured Resource | Highest-confidence resource category | Still not automatically a mine | 
| Ore Reserve | Economically mineable part of a Measured or Indicated Resource | Financing, permits or construction | 
| Producing mine | Permitted operation mining and processing ore commercially | That production cannot be suspended or become uneconomic | 
Climbing from the bottom to the top means passing a series of separate tests:
- Exploration: drilling shows continuity, grade and volume.
- Resource modelling: the data supports a compliant classification.
- Metallurgy: the valuable minerals can be recovered at acceptable cost.
- Engineering: mining, water, waste and infrastructure plans work.
- Economics: prices, costs and financing support the project.
- Permitting: environmental, land-use, water, heritage and mining approvals are granted.
- Construction and commissioning: the mine and plant operate reliably and production is sustained.
Worked examples: Per Geijer and Norra Kärr
According to its 2025 resource report, LKAB lifted the iron and phosphorus resource at Per Geijer, near Kiruna, to about 1.3 billion tonnes, containing about 2.2 million tonnes of rare earth oxides in situ. SGU’s September 2025 newsletter reported the rare earth figure rising from about 1.7 million tonnes. The rare earth component is an Inferred Mineral Resource under PERC 2021, and it sits beside existing mining infrastructure.
Correct wording: “reported inferred Mineral Resource”, not “producing rare earth mine”.
Norra Kärr in Småland tells a different story. A 2021 preliminary economic assessment was based on about 110 million tonnes at about 0.5% total rare earth oxides, but no current compliant classification was found in the material reviewed. Its earlier mining lease was revoked, a new concession application went in during December 2024, and a final decision remained outstanding in the sources found.
Other rare earth occurrences confirmed by SGU chemical analyses stay occurrences unless a compliant statement supports them. Before drawing any conclusion, ask which rung a number sits on.
Sweden is not alone in this pattern; Argentina’s rare earth gap shows another jurisdiction with large identified and modelled oxide tonnage but zero commercial production, where the barrier is legal rather than geological.
Where do lithium, cobalt, nickel and EU policy fit in?
The ladder is tidy. The real picture is messier, because policy designation, geology and actual status can each point in a different direction.

high_priority_articles.summary: Starmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changes  The GuardianSir Keir Starmer: Europe can't rely on US to 'bankroll' defence, Dublin event told  BBCEurope ‘must be ready’ to face security threats, warns Keir Starmer in Dublin  The Irish TimesKeir Starmer makes first major intervention since quitting as prime minister  The National ScotStarmer warns ‘Europe must wake up’ and sounds alarm over NATO’s dangerous defence gap  Lond...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner, Keir Starmer has said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10.
The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already.
“A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events.
“First, when Russia’s attack on Ukraine exposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.”
Starmer had called for closer European ties before stepping down as prime minister in July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”.
He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”.
Starmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit.
“I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.
“That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.”
His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham said that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU.
Next month, Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summit where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus.
Burnham has also said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility.
Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence.
“Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leading Nato member. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine.
“Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”

source_detail.name: Tuoi Tre News | The News Gateway to Vietnam

high_priority_articles.full_text:
According to India's BusinessLine, electronics manufacturers, particularly makers of smartphones and true wireless stereo (TWS) earbuds, have stepped up imports from Vietnam as memory chip prices have nearly quintupled over the past year.
Industry sources expect the trend to continue gaining momentum this year.
Citing Indian government data, BusinessLine reported that the value of India’s imports of electronic goods from Vietnam reached US$5.36 billion in fiscal year 2025-26, up 9.5 percent from approximately $4.9 billion a year earlier.
Imports of these products had previously reached $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2023-24, up 16.1 percent from $3.88 billion in fiscal year 2022-23.
According to several industry sources, many companies have taken advantage of zero import duties on eligible goods from Vietnam to bring in large volumes of smartphone components and other electronic products over the past year.
A veteran industry expert said components such as screens, camera modules and even Bluetooth earphones were being imported from Vietnam at zero tariffs.
The expert said most importers were Chinese companies with manufacturing or assembly facilities in India. Rather than importing directly from China, these businesses are increasingly sourcing components from Vietnam.
Some companies have also been importing TWS earbuds directly from Vietnam because doing so is significantly cheaper than manufacturing them in India. Others have even opted to build factories in Vietnam instead of India.
Under the ASEAN-India Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA), electronic goods imported from Vietnam may qualify for preferential tariffs if they meet rules of origin requirements and are accompanied by valid certificates of origin (C/Os).
This mechanism allows eligible products to enjoy preferential rates instead of most-favored-nation (MFN) tariffs, which generally range from 0 to 20 percent for most electronic products.
Investing in screen manufacturing facilities in India under production incentive schemes may qualify companies for incentives of 4 percent. By contrast, importing the same products from Vietnam at zero tariffs could offer higher profit margins without requiring companies to invest in factories in India.
Vietnam's electronics exports post strong growth
According to figures from the General Department of Vietnam Customs released by the Ministry of Industry and Trade on Saturday, as of October 15, 2026, exports of computers, electronic products and components, as well as phones and components, had reached $189.65 billion, accounting for around 40 percent of Vietnam's total export turnover.
Exports of computers, electronic products and components alone amounted to $135.31 billion, up 65.2 percent year on year.

high_priority_articles.title: Welded Stainless Line and Pressure Pipe From India, the Republic of Türkiye, and the United Arab Emirates: Postponement of Preliminary Determinations in the Less-Than-Fair-Value Investigations
high_priority_articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
                    DATES:
Applicable November 2, 2026.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
                    On August 4, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) initiated less-than-fair-value (LTFV) investigations of imports of welded stainless line and pressure pipe (welded stainless pipe) from India, Türkiye, and the UAE.[] 
                    
                     Currently, the preliminary determinations are due no later than December 22, 2026.
                
Postponement of Preliminary Determinations
Section 733(b)(1)(A) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), requires Commerce to issue the preliminary determination in an LTFV investigation within 140 days after the date on which Commerce initiated the investigation. However, section 733(c)(1)(A)(b)(1) of the Act permits Commerce to postpone the preliminary determination until no later than 190 days after the date on which Commerce initiated the investigation if: (A) the petitioner makes a timely request for a postponement; or (B) Commerce concludes that the parties concerned are cooperating, that the investigation is extraordinarily complicated, and that additional time is necessary to make a preliminary determination. Under 19 CFR 351.205(e), the petitioner must submit a request for postponement 25 days or more before the scheduled date of the preliminary determination and must state the reasons for the request. Commerce will grant the request unless it finds compelling reasons to deny the request.
                    On October 23, 2026, the petitioners [] 
                    
                     submitted a timely request that Commerce postpone the preliminary determinations in these LTFV investigations.[] 
                    
                     The petitioners stated that they request postponement “given the size and complexity of these investigations, the number of participating respondents, and the numerous extensions of time received by respondents to submit responses to Commerce's initial questionnaire. Postponement of the preliminary determinations will allow the petitioners adequate time to analyze and comment on the respondents' questionnaire responses and develop a comprehensive record in these investigations that the petitioners can then comment on in advance of Commerce's preliminary determinations.” [] 
                    
                
                    For the reasons stated above and because there are no compelling reasons to deny the request, Commerce, in accordance with section 733(c)(1)(A) of the Act, is postponing the deadline for the preliminary determinations by 50 days (
                    i.e.,
                     190 days after the date on which these investigations were initiated). As a result, Commerce will issue its preliminary determinations no later than February 10, 2027. In accordance with section 735(a)(1) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.210(b)(1), the deadline for the final determinations of these investigations will continue to be 75 days after the date of the preliminary determinations, unless postponed at a later date.
                
This notice is issued and published pursuant to section 733(c)(2) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.205(f)(1).
                    Dated: October 28, 2026.
Scot Fullerton,
Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Operations.
